title: Woodblocks: Printing a Whole Page at Once
summary: In China, people learned to carve a whole page of writing backwards into a block of wood, ink it, and press paper on top. Suddenly one carved block could make hundreds of copies! The oldest printed book with a date on it, the Diamond Sutra from the year 868, was found hidden in a secret cave.

sections.heading: Stamps, Seals and Stone Copies
paragraphs: Imagine you are a clerk in an office in China about 1,500 years ago. On your desk sits a little square seal carved from jade or bronze. When you dip it in red paste and press it onto a document, your official's name appears, perfectly, every single time. You have done this a thousand times. Have you ever stopped to think that you are printing?

Most of the pieces needed for printing were sitting around in China long before anyone printed a book. Seals were the first piece. Chinese officials, merchants and artists had used carved seals for well over a thousand years. A seal is carved in reverse, so that when it is pressed down the characters come out the right way round. That trick, carving a mirror image, is the very heart of printing. But a seal is small. It can say a name, not a whole page.

The second piece was the stone rubbing. In 175 CE, during the Han dynasty, scholars had the most important Confucian classics carved onto large stone tablets and set up outside the imperial academy in the capital, Luoyang, so that students everywhere would copy the correct, official wording. Later, people discovered a clever way to copy carved stones without writing anything. They laid damp paper over the stone, pressed it gently into the carved grooves, and then dabbed ink over the surface with a pad. The ink touched only the flat parts of the stone, so the carved characters came out as white letters on a black background. A rubbing was a perfect copy of the stone, made in minutes.

The third piece was paper itself, which you met earlier in this story. By the 600s CE, paper was common and cheap in China. And the fourth piece was ink. Chinese ink was made from soot, collected from burning pine wood or oil, mixed with animal glue and pressed into sticks. Ground up with water on an inkstone, it made a rich black liquid that soaked nicely into paper.

Seals carved in reverse, rubbings that copied a whole surface, cheap paper and good ink: put them all together and you get woodblock printing. Nobody knows the name of the person who first did it. It probably was not one person at all, but many carvers, monks and craftspeople trying ideas over many years. Historians think it was happening in China by the 600s or 700s, during the Tang dynasty, one of the richest and most outward-looking periods in Chinese history.

Cloth was printed even earlier. Pieces of silk with flower patterns stamped on them from carved blocks survive from the Han dynasty, before 220 CE. So people knew how to stamp a repeating pattern long before they used blocks to make whole pages of words.

sections.heading: How to Carve a Page Backwards
paragraphs: Let's step into a Tang dynasty print workshop and watch how a page is made. It is a quiet place. There are no big machines, no levers or screws. The most important tools are a sharp knife, a few chisels, a brush, a block of wood and a very steady hand.

Step one is the writing. A skilled scribe, chosen for beautiful handwriting, writes the text neatly on a sheet of very thin paper. Usually the page is laid out in columns, read from top to bottom and right to left, with lines ruled to keep everything straight.

Step two is the clever part. The block of wood is smoothed flat and brushed with a thin layer of paste, often made from rice. The carver lays the thin paper on top, face down. Because the paper is so thin, the ink shows through from the back, and now the characters can be seen in mirror image on the wood. The carver rubs the paper gently and may wet it, so that the ink of the characters sticks to the wood. When the paper is peeled or rubbed away, a backwards copy of the page is left on the block.

Step three is the long, slow carving. The carver cuts away every bit of wood that is not part of a character. When the work is done, the characters stand up from the surface like little ridges, raised a few millimeters above the hollowed-out background. Printers call this kind of surface relief, because the image stands up in relief. Carvers usually chose hard woods with a fine, even grain, such as pear or jujube wood, because they could hold tiny details without splitting. A single page might take a skilled carver a few days. Records from much later, in the 1600s, suggest a carver might finish around one hundred to one hundred and fifty characters a day.

Step four is printing, and this is surprisingly fast. The printer brushes water-based ink over the raised characters. A sheet of paper is laid carefully on top. Then the printer rubs the back of the paper with a dry, flat brush or pad, pressing it down onto the inked ridges. No press is needed. The paper is peeled off, and there is the page, with every character the right way round. The printer inks again, lays down another sheet, rubs, and peels. By some accounts, a skilled printer could make well over a thousand prints in a single day.

Notice something important: East Asian paper was thin and soft, so it was usually printed on only one side. To make a book, each printed sheet was folded in half with the blank side inside, and the folded sheets were stacked and sewn along the open edges. That is why old Chinese books have pages that are double-layered, with the fold at the outer edge.

There is also some sneaky science here. Water-based ink works beautifully on wood, because wood soaks up a little of the ink and then releases it evenly when paper presses down. Remember that, because in a later chapter you will see that this same ink did not work well on metal type, and a printer in Europe had to invent a different, oily ink.

sections.heading: A Charm in a Korean Pagoda
paragraphs: In October 1966, workers were repairing an old stone pagoda at Bulguksa, a famous Buddhist temple near the city of Gyeongju in South Korea. A pagoda is a tower-like monument, and this one, called Seokgatap, had been built around 751 CE, when the Silla kingdom ruled much of the Korean peninsula. Thieves had damaged the pagoda, and so experts took it apart to repair it.

Inside, in a hollow space in the stone, they found a reliquary, a special box for holy objects. And inside that, rolled up and partly damaged by centuries of damp and insects, was a narrow paper scroll printed with Chinese characters. It was a Buddhist prayer text called the Mugujeonggwang Great Dharani Sutra. A dharani is a kind of sacred chant or spell, which Buddhists believed could protect people and bring blessings. Making copies of such a text and placing them inside pagodas was thought to earn great merit.

The scroll is long and skinny: about 6.2 meters long, but only about 8 centimeters tall, so it would wrap around your arm many times. It was printed from woodblocks, and its characters are small and neat. Because it was sealed inside a pagoda finished around 751, it must have been printed before then. The text itself was translated into Chinese in about 704 or 705, so the print was almost certainly made sometime in the half-century between then and 751.

That makes it one of the oldest printed texts anywhere in the world. Some unusual character shapes in it were officially used in China only during the reign of Empress Wu Zetian, who ruled until 705, which helps support the early date. Historians do argue about one thing: where it was printed. Many Korean scholars believe it was printed in Silla, while some Chinese scholars think it was printed in China and carried to Korea. Either way, it shows that by the first half of the 700s, woodblock printing was being used to spread holy texts across East Asia.

It is a good reminder that the oldest surviving objects are not always the first ones ever made. The Bulguksa scroll survived because it was sealed away in stone. Countless other early prints were simply used, worn out, burned or thrown away.

sections.heading: One Million Tiny Pagodas
paragraphs: Now cross the sea to Japan, to the city of Nara in the 760s. Nara was Japan's capital then, full of grand Buddhist temples with sweeping wooden roofs. In 764 a dangerous rebellion broke out, led by a powerful minister called Fujiwara no Nakamaro, who is also known as Emi no Oshikatsu. The rebellion was crushed, and the ruler, Empress Shōtoku, wanted to give thanks and ask the Buddha for protection.

Her plan was enormous. She ordered one million small wooden pagodas to be made, each one about 21 centimeters tall, roughly the height of a school ruler standing on its end. They were turned on a lathe, a spinning tool for shaping wood, and painted white. Each pagoda had a hollow center, and inside each one was placed a tiny rolled-up paper strip printed with a Buddhist charm, or dharani. The project is known as the Hyakumantō Darani, which means 'one million pagoda dharani'.

Four different dharani texts were printed, each on a narrow strip of paper. Experts still argue about exactly how they were printed. Many think the printers used carved wooden blocks; others think they used plates cast from bronze or another metal. Either way, the job was printing, on an almost unbelievable scale for the time. The work took about six years, from around 764 to 770, and the pagodas were shared out among major temples, traditionally said to be ten.

Did they really make a full million? Historians are not completely sure, and some think 'one million' may have been a grand, round number. But hundreds of thousands were certainly made. Tens of thousands of the little pagodas still survive at Hōryū-ji, one of the temples that received them, which is also home to some of the oldest wooden buildings in the world. Many of the paper charms inside were lost over time, but thousands survive, nearly 4,000 at Hōryū-ji alone, and museums around the world, from Tokyo to New York and London, own a few.

The Hyakumantō Darani are among the oldest surviving printed texts whose date we know fairly well. They also show us something important about why early printing happened in East Asia. In Buddhism, copying holy words and spreading them was believed to bring blessings. The more copies, the more merit. Printing was the perfect tool for that: it made copying almost endless.

sections.heading: The Secret Library Cave
paragraphs: Our next stop is Dunhuang, an oasis town on the edge of the Gobi Desert in western China. For centuries it was a busy stop on the Silk Road, where camel caravans rested before crossing the deserts. Just outside the town, carved into a long cliff, are the Mogao Caves: hundreds of Buddhist cave temples filled with painted walls and statues, made between the 300s and the 1300s.

Around the year 1000, someone filled one small side-chamber of a cave with tens of thousands of old manuscripts, paintings and printed papers, and then sealed it up with a wall. Nobody is sure why. Maybe it was to protect them from invaders. Maybe it was a storeroom for worn-out holy texts, which could not just be thrown away. Then the hidden room was forgotten for about nine hundred years. The dry desert air kept the paper safe.

In 1900, a Taoist monk named Wang Yuanlu was looking after the caves and clearing away drifted sand. He noticed a crack in a painted wall, and behind it he found the sealed chamber, packed from floor to ceiling with scrolls. It held tens of thousands of items, perhaps as many as 50,000, in Chinese, Tibetan, Sanskrit, Uyghur and other languages. Today it is called the Library Cave.

In 1907 the explorer Aurel Stein, a Hungarian-born scholar working for British India, arrived at Dunhuang. He persuaded Wang Yuanlu, with payments of money, to let him take away thousands of manuscripts and paintings. Among them was one long printed scroll. Stein's way of getting these treasures is still hotly debated. Many people in China see it as taking away part of their heritage, and others later did the same, including the French scholar Paul Pelliot.

That scroll is the Diamond Sutra, now kept at the British Library in London. It is about five meters long, made of several panels of paper pasted together, and printed from carved woodblocks. At the start is a beautifully detailed picture: the Buddha sitting on a lotus throne under a canopy, speaking to an elderly disciple named Subhuti, surrounded by monks, guardian figures and even a pair of lions. It is one of the oldest dated printed illustrations in the world, and the carving is so fine that it shows woodblock printing was already a mature, skilled craft, not a new experiment.

At the very end of the scroll is a short note called a colophon. Translated, it says roughly that Wang Jie had this made, reverently, for free distribution to everyone, on behalf of his two parents. It also gives the date: the 15th day of the 4th month of the 9th year of the Xiantong reign period. In our calendar that is 11 May 868.

We know almost nothing else about Wang Jie. But because of his loving gift to his parents, his name sits on the oldest surviving printed book with an exact date. It is a book printed nearly 600 years before Gutenberg's Bible. And since the Diamond Sutra is so skillfully made, we know printing had been going on for a long time before it.

sections.heading: A Printing Boom in China
paragraphs: After the Diamond Sutra, the clues come thicker and faster. In the 800s, printed books were being sold in market towns, especially in Sichuan in the southwest and around the lower Yangtze River. Printers made calendars, almanacs for telling fortunes, dictionaries, Buddhist prayers and books on dreams and medicine. Printed calendars from the 870s and 880s were found in the Dunhuang cave too.

Calendars were such hot sellers that they caused trouble. In China, the calendar was official business: the emperor's astronomers decided the dates of festivals and the start of seasons. In 835, an official complained that private printers in Sichuan were selling their own calendars before the government's calendar came out, and the government ordered private calendar printing to stop. It may be one of the first attempts in history to control what people printed.

Then came a giant step. In 932, during a troubled time called the Five Dynasties, a senior minister named Feng Dao began a project to print the whole set of Confucian classics, the books every student and official had to know. Scholars carefully checked the text against the stone classics. The work took more than twenty years, until the 950s. For the first time, the most important books for government and education were printed officially, so that students across the country could own exactly the same, correct text.

Under the Song dynasty, which began in 960, printing exploded. Between 971 and 983, craftsmen in Chengdu in Sichuan carved the Kaibao Tripitaka, the complete collection of Buddhist scriptures, using about 130,000 woodblocks. Printed books of history, poetry, medicine, farming and mathematics followed. Government offices, Buddhist temples and private businesses all printed. Some Song printing houses became family firms lasting generations.

One famous writer of the Song dynasty, the poet Su Shi, noted in the 1070s that older scholars had struggled to find copies of books, but that now merchants were printing all kinds of books and producing huge numbers of pages every day. Students had more books than ever, he said, though he grumbled that they did not read them as carefully as before! Every age, it seems, has someone worrying that easy books make lazy readers.

sections.heading: Eighty-One Thousand Blocks in the Mountains
paragraphs: Our last stop in this chapter is Haeinsa, a Buddhist temple on the slopes of Mount Gaya in South Korea. Climb the stone steps at the top of the temple and you reach two long, plain wooden halls. Through their slatted windows you can glimpse rows and rows of wooden shelves, and on them, standing on their edges like books in a giant library, are about 81,000 carved woodblocks. Together they are called the Tripitaka Koreana, and they are the most complete set of Buddhist scriptures carved in wood that survives anywhere in the world.

The story behind them is dramatic. Korea, then ruled by the Goryeo dynasty, had carved an earlier set of Buddhist scripture blocks in the 1000s. But in 1232 Mongol armies invaded, and that first set was destroyed by fire. The Korean court had fled to Ganghwa Island to escape the Mongols. King Gojong ordered a complete new set to be carved, hoping that this huge act of devotion would win the Buddha's protection for the country.

The carving took place mostly between about 1237 and 1248. Teams of carvers prepared each block with great care. Tradition says the wood was birch, but scientific studies suggest much of it came from wild cherry and pear trees. Tradition also says the logs were soaked and boiled, then slowly dried so it would not crack or warp. Each block is about 70 centimeters long and 24 centimeters high, a few centimeters thick, carved on both sides, and weighs around 3 kilograms. Each side has 23 lines of 14 characters. The handwriting is so even that people once believed a single person carved it all, but historians now think a team of about thirty skilled carvers did the work. The whole collection holds around 52 million characters and weighs about 280 tonnes.

It was also edited very carefully. A monk named Sugi compared different versions of the scriptures and corrected errors, writing a long record of his changes. People often say the Tripitaka Koreana has no mistakes at all, but that is a myth: careful modern checks have found some missing or wrong characters. It is still astonishingly accurate for so many millions of hand-carved characters.

In 1398 the blocks were moved to Haeinsa, and they have stayed there for more than 600 years. Their storage halls, called Janggyeong Panjeon, are a marvel of science without machines. The windows on each side are different sizes, placed to let air flow through and keep the blocks dry. The floors are made of earth mixed with charcoal, lime and salt, which soak up moisture when the air is damp and give it back when it is dry. The halls survived wars and even a fire in 1817 that burned much of the temple. Experts once moved some blocks into a modern building with air conditioning, as a test, but they started to suffer, so the old halls were trusted again.

The blocks are on UNESCO's Memory of the World Register, and the halls are a UNESCO World Heritage Site. And here is the amazing thing: the blocks can still print. Because a woodblock keeps its whole page ready, it can be inked and printed again centuries later. That is one of woodblock printing's great strengths.

sections.heading: Why Woodblocks Worked So Well
paragraphs: Woodblock printing had some big advantages. It was cheap to start: you did not need a big machine, just wood, knives, brushes, paper and ink. It could print anything the carver could cut: complicated Chinese characters, pictures, maps, diagrams and decorations, all on the same block. And the blocks could be stored. A publisher could print fifty copies this year, put the blocks on a shelf, and print fifty more when people asked for them, without setting anything up again.

This mattered a great deal for Chinese, which uses thousands of different characters. An everyday reader might know a few thousand characters, and a scholar many more. Carving a page as one block meant the carver simply cut whatever characters were needed. There was no need to keep a huge stock of separate pieces, sorted and ready.

But there were weaknesses too. Carving was slow: a long book could need thousands of blocks and years of work. Blocks took up a great deal of space. Wood could crack, warp, rot or be eaten by insects, and fires were a constant danger. And if a carver made a mistake, fixing it meant cutting out the wrong character and fitting in a little plug of wood with the right one.

All over East Asia, woodblock printing remained the most common way to make books for well over a thousand years, right into the 1800s. In Japan, woodblocks were later used to make the famous colorful ukiyo-e prints, like Hokusai's Great Wave. Even today, artists carve and print woodblocks by hand. The idea that began with seals and stone rubbings turned out to be one of the longest-lasting technologies humans have ever made.

Still, think about that carver bent over the block, cutting character after character, day after day, and then doing it all again for the next page, and the next, for thousands of pages. A single slip of the knife could spoil a day's work. Carving a whole new block for every page was slow. And in the middle of the 1000s, a clever commoner in China looked at all those carved pages and asked a brilliant question: what if each character was its own tiny piece?

deepDive: Why did printing start in East Asia rather than somewhere else? Historians point to a combination of conditions rather than a single genius. China had cheap paper centuries before most of the world, a long tradition of carved seals and stone inscriptions, a state that valued standard texts for its examinations and administration, and Buddhism, whose teachings promised merit for multiplying sacred words. Dating the very first print is hard, because early prints were cheap everyday items that rarely survived. The oldest survivors are religious objects that were deliberately sealed away: the Bulguksa dharani (between about 704 and 751), the Hyakumantō Darani (about 764 to 770) and the Diamond Sutra (868). There are scholarly debates around each. For the Bulguksa scroll, Korean and Chinese scholars disagree on whether it was printed in Silla or in Tang China and imported. For the Hyakumantō Darani, specialists argue whether the charms were printed from wooden blocks or metal plates, and whether a full one million were really produced. For the Diamond Sutra, the debate is ethical rather than technical: Aurel Stein's removal of Dunhuang manuscripts in 1907, partly through payments to the cave's caretaker, is regarded by many in China as a loss of national heritage, and today the International Dunhuang Project works to reunite the scattered collections digitally. The economics of woodblocks also deserve attention. Most of the cost was paid once, in carving; after that, each extra copy needed only paper, ink and a few seconds of rubbing. Because blocks could be stored and reprinted on demand, publishers did not have to guess how many copies to make in advance. That is one reason woodblock printing remained the main printing method in China, Korea and Japan until the 1800s, even after movable type was invented there. Finally, scale matters for judging impact: by the Song dynasty, official, temple and commercial printers together were producing books on a scale no hand-copying culture could match, centuries before Europe printed its first page.
funFact: The Tripitaka Koreana woodblocks at Haeinsa are carved with about 52 million characters, and after more than 750 years they can still be inked and printed.
